The two stages

One or two sentences: what stage 1 proves, and what stage 2 replaces or adds.

Stage 1 carries no marks of its own, but it must be demonstrated on time: it is the checkpoint that shows your group is on track. The project is graded once, at stage 2, out of 100. See Submission & grading.

Stage 2 requirements Final

What replaces the stage 1 approach, and what the finished system must do. The demo and grading are based on this list.

#Requirement
R1Observable behaviour, testable in a demo.
R2Required technique (e.g. timer interrupt, table in program memory).
R3A measurable accuracy or timing limit.

Deliverables. Commented source and a live demo of R1–Rn. There is no written report: every member answers oral questions about the code during the demo.

Background

Only the facts they cannot look up quickly: a formula, a hardware constraint, a rate. Link the Wiki instead of repeating it, and leave the design decisions to them.

Design notes

How you structure the program is entirely up to you. These are questions worth answering before you write much code, not a required design:

  • An open question about what belongs where.
  • An open question about what could go wrong, with no answer given.

Milestones

Show each milestone to the lab instructor as you reach it. Milestone 0 is the stage 1 checkpoint; the rest belong to stage 2.

  1. Stage 1 checkpoint. Meets S1–Sn.
  2. First mechanism. Measurable check-off criterion.
  3. Complete system. Meets R1–Rn.

Bonus (up to +10)

  • Extension: something that reuses the same mechanism for more credit.

Oral questions

There is no written report. Instead, 40 of the 100 marks come from the oral questions: at the demo, each member of the group is questioned individually about the program you submitted. Marks are given for your own answers, so every member must understand the whole program, not only the part they wrote.

You may keep your source in front of you. Expect questions of these kinds:

  • Your numbers. Where a value came from, recalculated at the desk for a case the examiner names.
  • Your data. Explain your own encoding or structure, and read part of it back.
  • Your code path. Walk through what happens, step by step, and say why each instruction is there.
  • Your measurements. What you measured, how far off it was, and what you changed.
  • Change it now. Which line would you edit to change X? Do it, rebuild and show us.
  • Break it. What would happen if this instruction were removed?
  • Stage 1 against stage 2. What the processor can do now that it could not do before.

You are responsible for every line you submit, including anything adapted from an example or written by another member of your group. “My teammate wrote that part” does not earn marks.

Submission & grading

Stage 1 is a required checkpoint: submit your source and demonstrate S1–Sn in the lab. It carries no marks, but a group that misses it cannot demonstrate stage 2 until it is shown.

Stage 2 is graded out of 100. Submit your commented source, demo the project live, and answer the oral questions individually. Submission method: TBA.
